name: The Veblen Effect
statement: For some status goods, demand rises as the price rises, because the high price is the point.
statementAccent: the high price is the point
meaning: The Veblen effect is the phenomenon in which demand for certain luxury or status goods increases as their price rises, in apparent contradiction of the law of demand. For such 'Veblen goods', a higher price signals prestige, exclusivity, and the buyer's wealth, so it makes the good more desirable rather than less. Over a range of prices the demand curve can slope upward. The good is bought not chiefly for its function but as a visible marker of status through conspicuous consumption, and cheapening it would undercut the very quality buyers seek.
mechanism: The good is purchased for the status it signals, and the price itself is the signal. A high, conspicuous price advertises quality, exclusivity, and the means to pay, adding to the buyer's utility in a way distinct from the good's practical usefulness. Because raising the price strengthens that signal, demand can rise as price rises over some range. The behaviour is rooted in Veblen's idea of conspicuous consumption, the display of spending to acquire or keep social standing, so the good functions as evidence of wealth in a contest of pecuniary emulation among rivals.

examples.text: Designer handbags, luxury watches, fine champagne, and prestige cars are commonly cited cases where a higher price can raise, rather than lower, desirability.
Cutting the price of a status good can reduce its appeal by weakening the signal of exclusivity, so demand may fall as the price falls over a range.
Harvey Leibenstein formalised the effect alongside the bandwagon effect, where demand rises because others buy, and the snob effect, where it falls because others buy.

variants.name: Snob and bandwagon effects
variants.text: Related demand interdependencies Leibenstein modelled together: the snob effect, where demand falls as more people consume a good, and the bandwagon effect, where it rises, both driven by others' consumption rather than by price.

variants.name: Conspicuous consumption
variants.text: Veblen's original concept, the display of wealth through spending to signal or maintain status, of which the price-driven Veblen effect is the formalised economic expression.

whyItMatters: It is central to the marketing of luxury and premium goods, where prestige pricing deliberately sets high prices to signal status, and to behavioural economics and the theory of positional or status goods. It also anchors a broader critique of consumerism descending from Veblen's satire of the leisure class. By showing that price can act as a signal rather than merely a cost, it complicates the law of demand and illuminates why some markets reward exclusivity over affordability.

working.text: for status goods, treat a high price as part of what buyers want, signalling exclusivity and wealth, not just a cost to be minimised.
expect the upward-sloping demand only for a subset of goods over a limited price range, reversing beyond it.
distinguish the Veblen effect, driven by price, from the snob and bandwagon effects, driven by how many others consume.

limits: The effect applies to a subset of goods over a limited price range, not universally; even for luxuries the upward slope reverses once the price climbs far enough. It is distinct from the snob and bandwagon effects, which turn on others' levels of consumption rather than on price. And genuine upward-sloping demand is empirically hard to establish: the testability of the effect has been questioned, in part because research participants may not report their status motives honestly. It is best treated as a real, documented tendency for luxury goods rather than a clean, universally measured law.
misreadings: It is not a property of goods in general; only a narrow subset of status goods behaves this way, and only over a limited range. It is not the same as a Giffen good: Giffen behaviour arises from income and substitution effects, typically for an inferior staple with no close substitute among poorer consumers, whereas the Veblen effect arises from status signalling. And it is not identical to the snob or bandwagon effects, which depend on how many others consume the good rather than on its price.
origin: Named after the economist and sociologist Thorstein Veblen, whose 'The Theory of the Leisure Class' (1899) introduced conspicuous consumption; the price-driven 'Veblen effect' was formalised as an economic concept by Harvey Leibenstein in his 1950 paper on bandwagon, snob, and Veblen effects.

sources.text: Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899). — conspicuous consumption and the display of wealth for status.
Veblen good, Wikipedia. — the upward-sloping demand curve, price as a status signal, and the distinction from Giffen, snob, and bandwagon effects.
